grade.first_break: In the necessity argument, the solution infers from T1,T2 ∈ W that each child must already contain an angle in S. Only the forward implication—containing an angle in S implies membership in W—was proved, so this inference is invalid.
grade.summary: The claimed characterization is correct, and the sufficiency construction is essentially rigorous. However, the necessity proof has a decisive logical gap: winning triangles need not themselves contain marked angles. The four-case analysis only proves that every cut of a safe triangle has a safe child; an additional induction on the finite winning derivation is required to conclude that no safe triangle is winning. This is a new argument, so the proof is capped at 3.
strengths: Correctly identifies the answer θ = 180°/n for integers n ≥ 2.
Correctly proves that a triangle containing kθ is winning by splitting that angle into θ and (k−1)θ.
The sufficiency interval argument correctly produces complementary multiples kθ and (n−k)θ, and handles n=2.
The four cases in the safe-triangle obstruction correctly show that both children cannot contain marked angles when the parent is safe and 180°/θ is nonintegral.

errors.description: The necessity proof reverses the established implication: T_i ∈ W does not imply that T_i contains an angle in S. To finish, one must use structural induction (or minimal winning depth) together with the fact that every cut has a safe child.
The proposed safe starting example incorrectly excludes θ=120°. Under the nonintegrality hypothesis, the equilateral triangle is safe for every such θ: if 60°=kθ, then 180°/θ=3k would be an integer.

grade.first_break: In the n≥3 sufficiency argument, the claim that C∉S and C≥60° imply C>60° is false when n>3; for example, C=60° need not belong to S.
grade.summary: The proposed solution reaches the correct characterization and supplies essentially complete sufficiency and necessity arguments. Its two local interval/inequality errors are readily repaired using facts already present, without any new mathematical argument.
strengths: Correctly proves by induction that any triangle containing a positive integral multiple of θ is winning.
For integral 180°/θ, the interval argument correctly reduces an arbitrary triangle to two triangles containing complementary multiples of θ.
For nonintegral 180°/θ, the four-case analysis exhausts how both children could contain marked angles and yields the required invariant.
The finite-strategy interpretation and all cases n≥2 are addressed.

errors.description: For n≥3, C∉S does not always imply C>60°. The needed conclusion C>θ still follows from the written facts: if n=3, nonmembership excludes C=60°; if n>3, θ<60°≤C.

For a cut from A to BC, the stated range of φ=∠APC is incorrect: it is (B,180°−C), not (C,180°−B). Equivalently, the stated interval is the range of ∠BPA. Either corrected interval contains 90° because both B and C are acute.
